name: Light Art Museum (LAM)
description: The Light Art Museum, known as LAM, occupies the 1890s Hold Street Market Hall designed by Győző Czigler. It is built around light as an art form, with works by pioneers such as László Moholy-Nagy and contemporary artists. A June 2026 report announced a temporary closure, but the museum's site now lists a new exhibition, EGO, from October 2026; check it for current status.

children.text: The Light Art Museum, or LAM, is at Hold utca 13 in Budapest's fifth district, inside a former market hall. The hall was built between 1892 and 1896 to plans by Győző Czigler as Market Hall No. 5, one of six large market halls built in Budapest in that era. Its eclectic structure covers about 2,107 square metres, and the museum keeps the hall's industrial character rather than hiding it.

The museum presents itself as a space dedicated to light as an independent art form, and one local article called it the world's first light art museum. Coverage from its first season lists around thirty-five works, including holograms, laser installations, animations, shadow and light objects and interactive pieces that visitors can approach closely.

The reviews and previews name some of the historic anchors. These include László Moholy-Nagy's 1931 light-space modulator, a kinetic sculpture that light projections were cast onto, and works by György Kepes and Victor Vasarely. Alongside them are contemporary pieces, such as Kiégő Izzók's Re-Fracture, an installation of sixty high-power tubes synchronised to music.

The best-known sight is a huge inflatable zeppelin hanging in the main hall, with animations and projections on its interior. A sponsored article about the first exhibition describes a balloon about forty metres long and roughly 2,000 square metres of textile surface, so treat those numbers as promotional.

Status needs care. A June 2026 article reported that the museum was temporarily closing at the end of June 2026 as its exhibition More than Human ended, with no date for a full reopening; the museum's own website and an October 2026 We Love Budapest article later described a new exhibition, EGO, running from October 2026. A March 2026 guide still described it as operating. Check the museum's own website for the current situation before planning a visit, and if you are sensitive to flashing lights or loud sound, ask the staff about the exhibits before you go in.
Good to know
Check the official LAM site (lightartmuseum.hu) first: a June 2026 report announced a temporary closure, but the site now lists a new exhibition, EGO, from October 2026.
Arany János utca on the M3 metro line is the nearest metro station named by one visitor guide.

A March 2026 Xpatloop guide advises that visitors with light sensitivity should check with staff for a safe route through the exhibits, because some installations involve strobe lights and loud audio; the museum's own site does not mention this.
Flash photography is not allowed according to visitor guidance; read the rules on the official site.

historyIntro: The Light Art Museum occupies a market hall from the 1890s. Its story runs from a working food market through a renovation, a pandemic closure and a 2022 conversion to a museum of light, with a temporary closure announced for mid-2026.

historySections.heading: A market hall for central Pest

children.text: The hall at Hold utca 13 was built between 1892 and 1896 to plans by the architect Győző Czigler as Market Hall No. 5, one of six large market halls built in Budapest in the Austro-Hungarian era. Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as eclectic, covering 2,107 square metres, with 190 permanent and 80 temporary stalls, plus police and ambulance rooms, a coffee-measuring point and a market supervision office. A restaurant and a meat-inspection building were attached.

The hall was renovated in 2014 and renamed Belvárosi Piac, the Inner City Market, and gradually became a producers' market. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, declining tourism during the COVID-19 pandemic led to a temporary closure from 1 January 2021. A local article on the museum recalls that the hall had once been a place where people bought produce, fish and meat, and that this activity had ended.

historySections.heading: From market to museum of light

children.text: The building reopened to visitors in September 2022 as the Light Art Museum Budapest, according to We Love Budapest and a sponsored report; Hungarian Wikipedia gives both summer 2022 and November 2022, so the exact start is unclear. An opening show, The Revolution of Light, featured work by György Kepes, László Moholy-Nagy and Victor Vasarely alongside contemporary Hungarian-origin artists, and was extended to 15 August 2023. A June 2026 article reported that the museum would temporarily close at the end of June 2026 and gave no reopening date; the museum's website and an October 2026 article later described a new exhibition, EGO, from October 2026, so check the official site for its current status.

name: Cinema Mystica Budapest
description: Cinema Mystica is an immersive audiovisual art space in the historic Párisi Udvar, at Ferenciek tere. Created by the digital artists of Global Illumination, it fills grand halls with projections, sound and interactive installations; its current show, Form in Flux, features works by 26 Hungarian and international artists.

children.text: Cinema Mystica is an immersive audiovisual art venue at Ferenciek tere 10, inside the historic Párisi Udvar. It was created by the digital artists of Global Illumination, and visitors are meant to interact with installations and projections rather than only watch them. A 2026 article puts the venue at over 1,200 square metres, spread through the building's grand halls.

The story began elsewhere. A May 2022 article describes an earlier Cinema Mystica show at Kristály Színtér on Margaret Island, with sixteen new-media installations. In July 2023 We Love Budapest reported the move into the Párisi Udvar as the country's first permanent immersive digital exhibition space, with 21 installations in ten rooms, 85 projectors and five kilometres of cable. An article in July 2026 marked the third anniversary and said more than 500,000 visitors had come.

The current main show is Form in Flux, Patterns of Consciousness, open since early summer 2025 with works by 26 Hungarian and international artists. Pieces named in coverage include The Visitors, four monumental human-shaped figures that respond to light and sound; All Eyes on You, a floor of eyes in a Flower of Life pattern that reacts to movement; and The Oracle, an LED chamber that generates an astrological reading from a visitor's birth date.

Other spaces include the Solfeggio Room, where sound-responsive visuals made in real time with TouchDesigner are projected onto four walls and the floor, and Futurama Budapest, an installation made for MVM Future Talks that takes visitors through the Budapest skyline up to the 27th century.

The setting is part of the appeal. The Párisi Udvar was restored over several years and reopened in 2019 as a hotel building, and Cinema Mystica uses its grand halls. Shows change over time, so what you see depends on the current programme.
Good to know
Booking online in advance is recommended because capacity is limited and the exhibition can sell out; check the official Cinema Mystica site for tickets and opening times.
The venue is accessed from Ferenciek tere in downtown Pest.
Exhibitions are renewed periodically, so check what is currently on before you go.
The Párisi Udvar arcade itself is worth a few minutes if you have time before or after your session.

historyIntro: Cinema Mystica began as a 2022 exhibition on Margaret Island and moved in 2023 to its present home in the Párisi Udvar, a Pest arcade that was restored and reopened as a hotel building in 2019.

historySections.heading: A first showing on Margaret Island

children.text: A May 2022 We Love Budapest article describes the first Cinema Mystica exhibition at Kristály Színtér, a cultural centre on Margaret Island, in a Bauhaus-style building that the article says was formerly a mineral water-bottling plant. It showed sixteen new-media installations that combined art and technology, including Let There Be Life, a room with video projected on the walls, ceiling and floor showing the origin of life. The article names the visual artist and musician Dávid Vígh (Takkra) and the visual group Glowing Bulbs among those involved, and does not identify the founders of Cinema Mystica.

The permanent home is in the Párisi Udvar at Ferenciek tere 10. According to We Love Budapest, the Downtown Savings Bank commissioned the architect Henry Schmahl, who conceived the building in 1912-1913, and it was one of Budapest's earliest reinforced concrete buildings. According to Hungarian Wikipedia it became a listed monument in 1976 (a 2018 We Love Budapest article gives 1967 for heritage protection), and the arcade stood largely empty for years; the Jégbüfé ice-cream parlour and a hologram shop were among its well-known tenants. Restoration began in 2014, and the building reopened as a hotel in The Unbound Collection by Hyatt, with the passage open to the public.

In July 2023 We Love Budapest reported that Cinema Mystica had moved into the Párisi Udvar as the country's first permanent immersive digital exhibition space, with 21 installations in ten rooms, 85 projectors and five kilometres of cable. By July 2026, the venue marked its third anniversary, reporting more than 500,000 visitors and four exhibitions so far. The current show, Form in Flux, has run since early summer 2025 with works by 26 Hungarian and international artists.

name: IKONO Budapest
description: IKONO Budapest is an immersive, interactive art experience at Váci utca 27, in the heart of the downtown shopping street. Its rooms include a ball pit, a mirror maze and a light-painting space, created with artists such as Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and it is part of a European IKONO network.

children.text: IKONO Budapest is an immersive art museum at Váci utca 27, on the main pedestrian shopping street of downtown Pest. It has been open since September 2023, and the idea is that visitors step into the art instead of only looking at it: touching, listening, moving and interacting are encouraged. The official site describes it as suitable for people of all ages.

The Budapest venue belongs to the IKONO Xperience network. According to We Love Budapest, the brand first opened in Madrid in 2020 and has since expanded to Rome, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. The official Budapest page lists Madrid, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin among the network's cities, so this is a format tried elsewhere rather than something designed only for Budapest.

Room counts depend on the source: the opening-week article spoke of ten fantasy worlds, while the official site now speaks of twelve rooms. Named experiences include the Lantern Sanctuary, where light and shadow create dreamlike scenes; a light-painting room inspired by Picasso's experiments with light; and The Love Within, an immersive work by the artist Koketit about self-love. Reviewers and press mention a large ball pit, a mirror maze and a Super Mario-themed room.

Rooms were created with international artists. The opening-week article names Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and the venue page for Budapest credits the American visual artist Heather Bellino with installations that invite visitors to look for hidden meanings, patterns and symbols. A walk through takes about an hour according to the same article.
Being on Váci utca, IKONO is easy to combine with a downtown walk. Sources give no details about the building itself, so treat this as an experience venue rather than a historic site.
Good to know
Check the official IKONO Budapest site for current opening times, tickets and booking conditions.
Wear comfortable clothes if you plan to try the ball pit, and check the official site for rules on bags and photography.
Váci utca is a pedestrian street in downtown Pest, so IKONO fits easily into a walk through the centre.

historyIntro: IKONO Budapest is the Hungarian branch of a young European network of immersive art museums. Its short history runs from a first venue in Madrid in 2020 to a Váci utca opening in September 2023.

historySections.heading: From Madrid to a European network

children.text: According to We Love Budapest, the IKONO brand first opened in Madrid in 2020 and then expanded to Rome, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. A September 2023 article said the first IKONO exhibit had opened in Madrid about three years earlier, with Rome and Barcelona following before Budapest. The official IKONO site presents Budapest as part of the IKONO Xperience network, which also has locations in Madrid, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. The sources consulted do not name the founders.

The Budapest venue is at Váci utca 27, on the pedestrian shopping street of downtown Pest, and has been open since September 2023. A We Love Budapest article published on 5 September 2023 described it as recently opened, with ten fantasy worlds including a colourful jungle, a large ball pool, a UV-painted sea installation, a light-painting room inspired by Picasso's experiments with light and a quiet room. Sources give no details about the building's earlier history.

The rooms were created with international artists. The opening article names Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and the venue profile says the Budapest venue was created with the American visual artist Heather Bellino. The official site now describes twelve rooms, naming experiences such as the Lantern Sanctuary, light painting and The Love Within, an immersive work by Koketit about self-love, so the programme has been extended since opening or is counted differently.
